source.title: Exact Gap between Generalization Error and Uniform Convergence in Random Feature Models
source.authors: Zi-Tong Yang; Yu Bai; Song Mei

page_placements.theme: Noisy interpolation generalizes only under stated conditions

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes uniform-convergence bounds and generalization for theoretical random-feature regression interpolators. Its noisy-response setting is not a test of the specified deep-network random-label training behavior or the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper states that the minimum-norm interpolator has zero empirical risk in the overparameterized regime and analyzes its population risk for noiseless and Gaussian-noisy responses. Those results use a random-feature model and do not test the listed claim versions. Results on uniform-convergence bounds U and T are omitted because they measure bounds, not the listed training behavior.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes uniform-convergence bounds for minimum-norm random-feature regression with linear signal plus Gaussian response noise. It does not test any listed version concerning deep networks trained on randomized labels, optimization dynamics, input corruption, or explicit regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's main paraphrase is accurate. Under the stated assumptions and proportional scaling, classical uniform convergence can diverge with sample size for noisy responses while uniform convergence over interpolators remains bounded. In noiseless regression, both bounds vanish but at slower rates than actual risk. The reported power laws are inferred from numerical evaluations of analytical expressions.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives a theoretical and simulation analysis of minimum-norm random-feature regression interpolators and uniform-convergence bounds. It does not reproduce deep-network training with stochastic gradient methods or randomized labels.

fits_no_version.finding: In the kernel limit of random-feature regression, inferred risk decays as ψ2⁻² without response noise. With fixed positive Gaussian response noise, excess risk decays as ψ2⁻¹ and the scaled squared interpolation norm grows as ψ2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm random-feature regression can interpolate noisy responses while its excess population risk vanishes as sample size grows in the specified high-dimensional limits.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite noiseless simulations compare empirical uniform-convergence quantities U and T with analytical predictions over 20 instances.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Analytical uniform-convergence predictions agree with finite random-feature regression simulations in the tested setting.

record.problems: The main results are asymptotic and rely on stated modeling and technical assumptions. The simulations described in the text use 20 instances and report spread as 1/√20 times the standard deviation; plotted values are not given numerically in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Uniform-convergence bounds U and T and their comparisons with risk are omitted because they measure bounds rather than the claim's training behavior. Figure 2 values are retained only as figure-only because the text does not state the numerical values.

untested.parts: All parts: SGD-trained deep networks, completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparisons and convergence speed across label-corruption fractions.
Deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and classification test-error degradation across randomly corrupted label fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Training dynamics distinguishing early learning of shared patterns from later memorization of noise.

record.verdict_notes: Zero empirical risk in this random-feature interpolation setup does not establish any listed deep-network random-label claim. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods; completely random labels; test error at chance; unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corrupted labels to all corrupted labels, training error across that sweep, and classification test error rising toward chance.
Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and their effects on fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Training-time evidence that real-data patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses memorization and generalization in overparameterized networks as motivation for studying uniform-convergence bounds, without testing the listed random-label claims.

tranche.reason: The study analyzes minimum-norm random-feature regression with linear signal and additive Gaussian response noise. Its results neither test the listed deep-network claim versions nor use random-label fitting as a tool.
